meta.label: Ride-hailing
meta.attribution: These are the ways a person in the United States gets a ride without owning a car or waiting for a bus: the two national gig-platform apps, two apps that book an already-licensed taxi instead of a gig driver, a taxi hailed on the street or called directly with no app at all, two driver-owned cooperatives, a company that employs its own drivers, a service built for children and other dependents, a service built for disabled and older riders, a phone-only service for people without a smartphone, a shared shuttle run with public transit agencies, and a fully driverless service. Public transit itself, meaning buses, trains and transit passes, is a separate decision on this site; this one covers on-demand, door-to-door rides. The core trade-off is price against how much of your data and history a company collects: the cheapest and most convenient routes are run by platforms that share ride data with advertising partners and, in Uber's case, paid a nine-figure settlement over a covered-up data breach, while the more private and driver-owned routes usually mean a smaller network and less company infrastructure behind you if something goes wrong. Sourced from company safety and privacy pages, the California legislature, New York City's Taxi and Limousine Commission, and the New York Attorney General; every score links its source and date. Not legal advice. Reviewed 2026-09. Dispute or correct any rating via Contribute.

criteria.label: Less data shared with advertisers or exposed in a breach
How the driver is classified, paid or owns a stake
Published safety record or driver screening
Reaches riders the standard apps miss

products.name: Uber
products.description: One of the two national gig-platform apps, booked entirely through its own network of independent-contractor drivers. Uber's own safety report and a fifty-state data breach settlement are both part of the public record in a way most other options here are not.

privacy.note: The New York Attorney General's 2018 release on the multistate settlement says Uber agreed to pay a record $148 million to all 50 states and Washington DC over a 2016 breach in which hackers downloaded the personal information of 57 million riders and drivers, including driver's license information for about 600,000 drivers nationwide. It says Uber paid the hackers $100,000 to conceal the breach and gave notice in late November 2017, a year after it happened, and that the settlement requires Uber to hire an outside party to assess its data security regularly.

labor.note: California law, as amended by Proposition 22, states that an app-based driver 'is an independent contractor and not an employee or agent' of the network company, as long as the company does not set the driver's schedule, require acceptance of specific ride requests, or block the driver from working for other apps or other jobs.

safety.note: Uber's own second US Safety Report, covering 2019 and 2020, recorded 3,824 reports across its five most severe categories of sexual assault and misconduct, a 38 percent decrease in the reported rate from the prior report period, and states that Uber's motor vehicle fatality rate is still half the national average.

products.name: Lyft
products.description: The other national gig-platform app, built on the same independent-contractor driver model as Uber. Lyft's privacy policy and safety report draw on the same kind of disclosure Uber's do, though the specific numbers and dates differ.

privacy.note: Lyft's privacy policy, last updated July 1, 2026, says 'We do not sell your personal information to third parties for money' and that 'no one can buy the personal information we collect from and about you,' but adds that Lyft 'may need to share your personal information with third parties to deliver relevant personalized ads to you on and off the Lyft Platform,' and that some of these disclosures 'may constitute "sharing" or the "sale" of personal information for "targeted advertising" purposes' under certain state privacy laws. The policy does not name the advertising partners.

labor.note: California law, as amended by Proposition 22, classifies app-based drivers, including those driving for Lyft, as independent contractors rather than employees, as long as the company does not set schedules, force acceptance of ride requests, or block drivers from working other jobs.

safety.note: Lyft's safety data disclosure, using the RALIANCE taxonomy for sexual assault and misconduct categories, recorded 615 reports of non-consensual touching of a sexual body part in 2022 alone, about 1 in every 880,000 rides that year, and 910 reports of attempted touching of a non-sexual body part, about 1 in 600,000 rides.

products.name: Curb
products.brand: app that books an already-licensed taxi
products.description: An app that books and pays for an already-licensed taxi instead of dispatching a gig driver. A rider can also use it to pay a driver they are already riding with, without having booked through the app first.

safety.note: Curb's own App Store listing says 'Curb works only with professional drivers. Every time you ride with Curb, you’ll ride with a fully licensed, insured driver.' The listing does not describe what background checks or vehicle inspections apply, and Curb publishes no safety record on that page.

focuses: Also pays for a hailed cab

products.name: Arro
products.brand: app that books an already-licensed taxi
products.description: A second app that books an already-licensed taxi, in six US metro areas, with a specific no-surge guarantee and a small flat service fee on top of the city-set meter fare.

economical.note: Arro says 'prices do not increase, regardless of weather, demand or conditions' because 'rates are set by the municipal jurisdiction in which the taxi company operates and not by Arro,' and adds a service fee of up to $2.00 for a ride booked through the app, which it says may be waived in some circumstances.

safety.note: Arro says its drivers 'go through extensive training and education and are locally licensed for your safety,' the same city licensing system Curb also relies on.

products.name: Licensed taxi, hailed or called directly
products.description: Flagging a cab on the street or calling a local taxi company, the way people got a ride before any app existed. New York City's fleet is used here as the best-documented example: its medallion taxis charge a fare the city itself sets and are not booked through Uber or Lyft, though many now also work with e-hail apps such as Curb and Arro. Most medallions are leased to drivers rather than owned by them, and the city now runs a debt-relief program for owners after medallion values collapsed.

economical.note: New York City's Taxi and Limousine Commission sets the metered taxicab fare directly: a $3.00 initial charge, $0.70 per additional unit, a $2.50 rush-hour surcharge and a $1.00 nighttime surcharge, plus fixed airport fares such as $70.00 to Kennedy Airport, effective December 19, 2022. The rate does not rise with demand the way an app's dynamic pricing can.

labor.note: New York City's Medallion Relief Program gives individual medallion owners grants of up to $20,000, and up to $9,000 more in hardship cases, to help them 'afford their medallion debt, so more owners can continue operating yellow taxis.' Most drivers lease a taxi or medallion rather than owning one, and a separate TLC rule caps what an owner can charge a driver who cancels a lease.

links.label: NYC TLC minimum pay rule for app-based drivers

products.name: The Drivers Cooperative
products.brand: driver-owned co-op, New York City and Denver
products.description: A driver-owned cooperative based in New York City that its homepage says specializes in paratransit and Non-Emergency Medical Transportation, and that lists Denver among the cities it is working to reach. It runs on an app like Uber or Lyft's, but the company is structured so members, not outside shareholders, keep what it earns.

economical.note: The Drivers Cooperative's homepage says its members 'make 8-10% more on each trip than on Uber and Lyft,' and quotes a New York Times description of the cooperative as intending 'to take a smaller commission than Uber or Lyft and charge riders a lower fare.' The page shows no rider fare comparison and carries a 2023 copyright line, so this score rests on the co-op's stated intention.

labor.note: The Drivers Cooperative's homepage calls itself 'a driver-owned cooperative' under the heading 'Drivers steer our company,' says its members 'make 8-10% more on each trip than on Uber and Lyft' and that 'profits go back to drivers as dividends,' and asks for donations to build 'the 100% worker-owned transportation company of the future.'

focuses: New York City and Denver only

products.name: Fare Co-op
products.description: A second driver-owned cooperative, operating in six states, and says it became America's third-largest fully licensed rideshare company less than a year after launching. Drivers can join as fractional owners for free or buy a full share for a bigger cut of the profit.

economical.note: Fare Co-op's homepage advertises 'No Surge Pricing' and 'Save 20% vs. Uber,' a saving the co-op states itself and does not support with a fare comparison on that page.

labor.note: Fare Co-op says drivers hold 50% of the ownership, and that 'Every driver can join as a Fractional Shareholder at no cost' and earn 55% of platform profits from day one, rising by 2% for every 10 customer referrals up to 85%. It says full shareholders earn 85 to 90% of profits on organic Fare Co-op rides.

products.name: Alto
products.description: A ride service that employs its own drivers and owns its own fleet instead of contracting with independent drivers in their own cars. Its site lists five US metro areas, and in Los Angeles and Miami its cars and W-2 drivers also appear inside the Uber app through Uber Black, Uber XL and UberTeen.

labor.note: Alto's homepage says 'Our W-2 drivers are trained professionals' and 'not gig workers,' with 'hourly pay, benefits, and opportunities for career development,' rather than independent contractors engaged through an app.

safety.note: Alto says its 'W-2 employee drivers are background checked, trained and continuously coached, plus AI-powered real-time video monitoring tracks performance.' Its site lists Dallas, Houston, Los Angeles, Miami and San Francisco, and says that in Los Angeles and Miami its vehicles and drivers also operate on the Uber platform through Uber Black, Uber XL and UberTeen.

products.name: HopSkipDrive
products.brand: booked by a guardian, for children and dependents
products.description: A ride service built for children and other dependents who need extra supervision, booked by a parent, guardian or school rather than by the rider. Its drivers, called CareDrivers, are vetted well beyond a standard rideshare background check.

safety.note: HopSkipDrive says CareDrivers complete a '15-point certification' that includes 'background and driving record checks' and 'caregiving experience verification,' and 'receive education in trauma-informed care and neurodiversity.'

products.name: Waymo One
products.description: A fully driverless ride-hailing service, so there is no human driver to classify, pay or vet. It runs in five US metro areas and publishes its own safety data hub that compares its crash rates with a human benchmark.

safety.note: Waymo's own safety data hub reports 271.3 million rider-only miles driven through June 2026, with 95 percent fewer crashes causing serious injury or worse, 82 percent fewer injury-causing crashes and 82 percent fewer airbag-deployment-in-any-vehicle crashes than a human benchmark for surface streets in the areas where it operates: Los Angeles, the San Francisco Bay Area, Phoenix, Austin and Atlanta. Waymo publishes and updates these figures itself, on the schedule of NHTSA's Standing General Order reporting.

products.name: Via
products.brand: on-demand shuttle run with a transit agency
products.description: An on-demand shuttle usually not booked under its own name: cities and transit agencies run it under their own brand, such as the Camden Loop in New Jersey, and riders share a vehicle with others heading the same way. It fills the gap between a fixed bus route and a private ride, at a fare set by the transit agency rather than by Via.

accessibility.note: Via says it works with '700+ partners across the world, from rural counties to large transit agencies,' to 'Fill the gaps in your network' and connect people to jobs, education and healthcare. Its homepage cites Sioux Falls, South Dakota (23% transit ridership increase), Fort Worth, Texas with Trinity Metro (86% reduction in excessively long paratransit rides) and Camden, New Jersey (72% more job access within 30 minutes) as results.

focuses: Booked under a transit agency's brand

products.name: GoGoGrandparent
products.brand: phone call only, no app needed
products.description: A phone-only service for people who do not want to, or cannot, use a smartphone app. Calling one number arranges an Uber or Lyft ride through a human or a touch-tone menu, at the underlying app's own fare plus GoGoGrandparent's own fee.

accessibility.note: GoGoGrandparent says 'everything works with a simple phone call. You don’t need an app or internet access,' and its call menu says 'PRESS 1 to request a ride pickup from your home,' with 'PRESS 0 to speak with an operator about anything else.' It says it arranges rides through partners including Uber and Lyft.

economical.note: GoGoGrandparent says 'You pay the standard Uber or Lyft fare plus a small service fee for coordination, monitoring, and support,' so a ride costs more than calling the underlying app directly.

focuses: Costs more than the app it books

products.name: UZURV
products.brand: scheduled rides for disabled and older riders
products.description: A ride service built for people with disabilities and older adults. It often works through partnerships with community programs, public transit agencies, paratransit providers, municipal governments and healthcare providers, each of which sets its own service areas and hours. Wheelchair-accessible vehicles are available where a partner program includes them.

accessibility.note: UZURV's riding page says it is a transportation network company that 'specializes in assisted mobility' for older adults, people with disabilities and others who want extra help, and offers Standard Service and Wheelchair-Accessible Vehicle Service, adding that 'Availability of UZURV WAV service varies by location.' It says it often partners with community programs, public transit agencies, paratransit providers, municipal governments and healthcare providers, and that each partner sets its own service areas, days, hours and fares. The page does not list cities.

safety.note: UZURV says drivers must pass 'national criminal and driving background checks' before providing trips and 'at-least annually thereafter,' must meet Federal Transit Administration substance abuse training and testing requirements 'for applicable programs,' and complete UZURV's driver credentialing, which covers the Americans with Disabilities Act and, in its words, 'appropriate techniques for transporting people with disabilities and older adults.'
